digests.narrative:
The week the theme repriced. AAOI's earnings became the sector's read-through document: management said it cannot make enough CPO lasers to take part in first-generation co-packaged deployments because capacity has to go to its own transceivers first, flagged a 20-40% demand imbalance, and expects full qualification of 1.6T products at a hyperscaler customer within weeks. MACOM's transcript supplied the independent corroboration the desk has been waiting for — customers arriving with urgency over a shortage of indium phosphide DFB lasers.

Layered on top is policy. A draft US rule would bar imports of new Chinese optical transceiver models, which would take share from Innolight and Eoptolink and hand it to Western suppliers. It is worth being exact about its status: it is a draft, nothing has been published in the Federal Register, and the agency could still modify or shelve it. A large part of this week's move is paying for it as though it were settled.

The counterweight sits inside AAOI's own release. Gross margin fell to 27.7% from 30.3% a year earlier and 29.1% last quarter while revenue grew 86%, which is not what a seller in a genuine shortage produces. And the $500m-plus fourth quarter circulating in the feed is call commentary against a company guide of $255-290m for Q3 and roughly $1.1bn for the year.
keyPoints: AAOI: cannot supply first-generation CPO lasers because own-transceiver demand takes priority
MACOM cites customers arriving with urgency over an indium phosphide DFB laser shortage
AAOI expects 1.6T qualification at a hyperscaler customer within weeks
Draft US rule would bar new Chinese transceiver models — unpublished, scope and timing unverifiable
AAOI gross margin fell to 27.7% from 30.3% year on year despite 86% revenue growth
The $500m+ Q4 figure is call commentary; guidance is $255-290m for Q3 and ~$1.1bn for the year

digests.narrative:
Allocation is now the whole story. DRAM and HBM capacity for 2027 is described as sold out across Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, NAND is sold out on current annual capacity, and customers are being allocated only 60-70% of the volumes they requested, with Kioxia and SK Hynix finalising the rest by August. The framing in the feed is that 2027 is the most severe point of the shortage.

Sandisk's fiscal fourth quarter turned that industry narrative into a company number: revenue of $8.97bn, adjusted EPS of $39.25, gross margin near 78%, first revenue recognised from the QLC-based Stargate platform, and a fiscal Q1 2027 guide of $10.3-10.8bn with $44-46 of EPS. That is the NAND-specific pricing evidence the desk had been holding out for.

What the theme cannot tell you is where in the cycle this sits. The shares trade at a single-digit multiple of guided earnings, which is the market pricing a peak the guidance does not show. He remains explicitly bullish on memory while noting the sector's attention has rotated to photonics — his own framing of a market that moves from bottleneck to bottleneck.
keyPoints: DRAM and HBM 2027 capacity described as sold out at Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix
Customers allocated only 60-70% of requested volumes; Kioxia and SK Hynix finalise by August
Sandisk fiscal Q4: revenue $8.97bn, adjusted EPS $39.25, gross margin near 78%
First revenue recognised from the QLC-based Stargate storage platform
Fiscal Q1 2027 guided to $10.3-10.8bn revenue and $44-46 EPS
Single-digit forward multiple says the market is pricing a cycle top the guide does not show

digests.narrative:
The quietest week of flow in the layer and the biggest change in the desk's positioning. TSMC appears in the feed only in passing — the Amkor ten-year packaging agreement, the NVIDIA deal, an aside about how the ticker is pronounced — while its own disclosure did the talking: first-half revenue up 35.6% year on year with June alone up 67.9%.

The structural point that matters for the whole map is that the advanced-packaging squeeze is loosening. Industry reporting has the CoWoS supply-demand gap narrowing from roughly 20% to 10% by the end of 2026, with capacity heading toward about 200,000 wafers a month by end-2027. That is why scarcity on this map keeps migrating upstream into lasers and substrates rather than staying in packaging.

GlobalFoundries and Intel are unchanged and unmentioned. The CHIPS silicon-photonics award remains GlobalFoundries' whole case, and Intel's disclosed 14A schedule still puts risk production in 2027 and volume in 2028.
keyPoints: TSMC first-half revenue up 35.6% year on year; June alone up 67.9%
CoWoS supply-demand gap reported narrowing from about 20% to 10% by end-2026
CoWoS capacity heading toward roughly 200,000 wafers per month by end-2027
TSMC is the only name in the book with monthly revenue disclosure
No new analyst theses on GlobalFoundries or Intel this week
Intel's disclosed 14A schedule: risk production 2027, high volume 2028

digests.narrative:
The notable development is whose side the analysis is on. The week's one substantive neocloud post is a guide to doing diligence on a Nebius short: read the hyperscaler prints first — record AI cloud demand, growing backlogs and improving margins at Google, Amazon and Meta — then compare that against what Nebius itself discloses.

The gap is the point. Nebius reports capacity fully contracted and capex guided to $20-25bn, but publishes no contracted megawatts, no delivery schedule and no customer names, against first-quarter revenue of $399m. The funding is convertibles, an NVIDIA equity stake and secured debt at SOFR plus 250 basis points, which makes the equity a levered call on execution rather than a compute business.

IREN carries the same structure with better counterparties and no fresh evidence this week. Both drop out of the desk's priority ranking as the flow thins; Nebius reports on 12 August, which is the next real test.
keyPoints: The week's only neocloud thesis is a framework for shorting Nebius, not owning it
Hyperscaler prints show record AI cloud demand, growing backlog and improving margins
Nebius discloses no contracted megawatts, delivery schedule or customer names
Q1 revenue of $399m against capex guided to $20-25bn
Funding is convertibles, an NVIDIA equity stake and secured debt at SOFR plus 250bps
Nebius Q2 results due 12 August

digests.narrative:
Two threads this week, and the louder one is policy. The White House committed direct investment to critical minerals: $400m to Sunrise Energy Metals for scandium, $25m to Westwater for graphite, $8m to 5E Advanced Materials for boron and $4.8m to Rare Element Resources for magnet rare earths, alongside private commitments. For this map it is a reminder that the upstream inputs to the buildout are now a state interest, though none of these are yet positions.

The second thread is a correction to a fear rather than a new fact. Viavi pushed back publicly on talk of CPO delays — the yield-driven slippage story is dismissed outright, with the process described as improving and moving forward. That matters because most of this map's photonics timing assumptions are downstream of whether CPO ships on schedule.

Amkor remains the layer's live position: record second-quarter net sales of $1.90bn led by computing and automotive rather than by AI packaging, with the advanced-packaging ramp still a 2028 story.
keyPoints: White House critical-minerals investments: $400m scandium, $25m graphite, $8m boron, $4.8m rare earths
Viavi dismisses CPO delay talk outright and describes the process as improving
Amkor record Q2 net sales of $1.90bn, led by computing and automotive rather than AI packaging
Amkor's advanced-packaging AI ramp remains a 2028 story with partial 2027 steps
FormFactor's CPO revenue commentary continues to confirm the packaging-side ramp
None of the newly funded minerals names are desk positions

digests.narrative:
The layer's news arrived second-hand, inside AAOI's earnings call, and it was a widening of the bottleneck rather than a resolution of it. Alongside lasers, AOI flagged DSP and TIA constraints — the signal-processing and amplifier silicon that sits inside every transceiver — which reads across to Semtech, MACOM and the broader analog suppliers.

This is the pattern the desk keeps finding: the shortage is not one component but a chain, and each earnings season names another link. The practical consequence is that transceiver revenue forecasts built purely on laser capacity are optimistic, because a module needs the DSP and the TIA too.

No dedicated positions here and no company disclosure from the named suppliers themselves — this remains a read-through from a customer's call, which is weaker evidence than the layer's importance deserves.
keyPoints: AAOI flagged DSP and TIA bottlenecks alongside the laser shortage
The read-through runs to Semtech, MACOM and the analog transceiver-component suppliers
Transceiver forecasts built on laser capacity alone understate the constraint chain
Evidence is a customer's earnings call, not disclosure from the suppliers themselves
No dedicated desk position in the layer
Marvell and Broadcom appear only in breadth lists this week

digests.narrative:
The week's genuine surprise was Aeva, a lidar company, signing a joint development agreement with an optical engine player for deployment at a major hyperscaler — which reframes it as a CPO and NPO optical source name rather than an automotive sensor one, and links it to the same laser supply chain the photonics book runs on. The shares reacted sharply after hours.

On humanoids, the comparables moved before the fundamentals. Unitree is listing at around $9bn against a $6.2bn March filing, with derivative markets implying a far higher open, while Agility Robotics arrives via de-SPAC later in Q4 at roughly $2.5bn pre-money. A flattering comparable is not an order book, and the FCC's reported move to bar Chinese humanoid and quadruped imports is protection rather than demand.

Nothing here has changed the desk's stance: robotics remains a venture-shaped exposure wearing public tickers.
keyPoints: Aeva signs a JDA with an optical engine player for deployment at a major hyperscaler
Aeva reframed as a CPO/NPO optical source name, linked to the same laser supply chain
Unitree listing at about $9bn versus $6.2bn in its March filing
Agility Robotics de-SPACs later in Q4 at roughly $2.5bn pre-money
FCC reported to be barring Chinese humanoid and quadruped imports — protection, not demand
No disclosed humanoid unit economics anywhere in the public comparables

digests.narrative:
AMD's quarter answered the question this desk actually has about the layer. Data-centre revenue was $6.7bn, up 107% year on year, and the 10-Q attributes it to EPYC processors and MI350-series parts — not to MI450. Helios entered production with shipments starting at the end of the third quarter, and the first gigawatt of the announced Anthropic deployment begins in the first half of 2027.

So the co-packaged optics read-through the feed keeps drawing from AMD's rack-scale roadmap to the laser suppliers is a 2027 event at the earliest, and the 2027 doubling is already the consensus case at the current price. That is three quarters of carry with nothing to prove it in between.

NVIDIA barely features this week beyond breadth lists, and its position is unchanged: management's own guidance is that supply stays constrained through the entire life of Vera Rubin, which is the demand hub underwriting the upstream bottleneck thesis. The offsetting fact is concentration — data centre is roughly 92% of revenue, sold to a handful of buyers.
keyPoints: AMD data-centre revenue $6.7bn, up 107%, attributed to EPYC and MI350 rather than MI450
Helios in production; shipments start at the end of Q3 2026
First gigawatt of the Anthropic deployment begins in H1 2027
The CPO read-through from AMD racks is a 2027 event at the earliest
NVIDIA management expects supply constraint through the entire life of Vera Rubin
NVIDIA data centre is roughly 92% of revenue, sold to a handful of buyers

digests.narrative:
The payers keep confirming demand and keep getting punished for funding it. Google Cloud backlog reached $514bn, up more than $50bn sequentially, with just over half expected to convert to revenue inside 24 months and cloud revenue up 82% to $24.8bn. Amazon raised capex to $220bn and said explicitly that even that will not meet 2026 demand, with 2027 the same. Meta narrowed full-year capex upward to $130-145bn.

The combined 2026 figure across the four now runs to roughly $720-745bn, and this is the cleanest demand signal on the map. But two qualifications belong on it. Part of the raises is memory cost inflation rather than incremental units, so the dollars overstate the pull on optics. And none of these companies disclose accelerator mix or capacity, so every read-through to a named supplier is inference.

The cash cost is now visible. Meta's free cash flow fell to $784m against $31.1bn of quarterly capex. Alphabet is the one whose spend is funded by an accelerating business, which is why it is the desk's accumulate leg here.

Just over half the Alphabet backlog is expected to convert to revenue within 24 months
Amazon capex raised to $220bn, with Jassy saying it still will not meet 2026 demand
Meta full-year capex narrowed upward to $130-145bn; quarterly free cash flow fell to $784m
Combined 2026 capex across the four now roughly $720-745bn
No hyperscaler discloses accelerator mix or capacity, so supplier read-throughs are inference
